_comment: Demo programme for the 2-day / 4-room Analyst Days grid. All talks are fictional. Loaded by seed.py only when the talk table is empty; interest_source/heavy_source are 'manual' because nothing scored them.

talks.title: Requirements that survive the roadmap
talks.abstract: Most specs die quietly three sprints after the kickoff. We walk through the four habits that kept a two-year payments initiative legible: a living glossary, a decision log with owners, a dated review cadence and one page per capability. The talk ends with a checklist you can apply to your own document set on Monday.

talks.title: Stakeholder maps in practice
talks.abstract: Influence and interest grids look tidy on slides and fall apart in a real steering committee. This session shows three worked maps from a logistics replatforming and one map that was wrong and why. Participants leave with a template and a habit for revisiting it mid-project.

talks.title: Analyst as translator, not gatekeeper
talks.abstract: When the analyst becomes the queue, the team slows down and the analyst burns out. We contrast two engagement models from the same company and the throughput of each. A short argument for pushing requirements work into the team and keeping the analyst on the hard seams.

talks.title: Event storming an accounting core
talks.abstract: A legacy general ledger has no reliable documentation and eleven years of folklore. We ran four event storming sessions with accountants, auditors and two engineers, and mapped the whole posting pipeline before writing a line of code. The talk covers the notation, the politics of the sticky notes and where the exercise failed.

talks.title: The long workshop format
talks.abstract: Eighty minutes is the shortest length that still lets a group disagree and recover. This is a guided walk through the facilitation script, the timing, the artefacts and the recovery moves when a workshop stalls. Expect a dense, hands-on session rather than a set of slides.

talks.title: Metrics the team can actually move
talks.abstract: Choosing three numbers and ignoring the other forty is harder than it sounds. We look at a delivery dashboard that nobody read and the much smaller one that changed behaviour. The method is borrowed from product analytics and adapted for internal platforms.

talks.title: Data contracts without a platform team
talks.abstract: Two analysts and one dbt project owned the schema for a year. This talk is the honest version of that story: the linting that helped, the review ritual that did not, and the two incidents that forced a change. Small-scale schema ownership, no vendor product required.

talks.title: Migration postmortems, honestly told
talks.abstract: Two failed cutovers, one successful retry and the same people throughout. We read the timelines together and pull out the four signals that were visible a week before each failure. A postmortem format that survives contact with management.

talks.title: BPMN that a business actually reads
talks.abstract: BPMN earns its keep when the business reads the diagram without a training course. We take one loan approval process and rewrite it three times: as modelled, as consumed, and as agreed. The gap between the three is the actual deliverable.

talks.title: Formal methods for the rest of us
talks.abstract: Invariants, temporal properties and model checking sound like a different discipline. This session reduces them to three questions any analyst can ask of a state machine and shows the answers on a permissions model. It is the densest talk of the programme and assumes comfort with set notation.

talks.title: API design review in ninety seconds
talks.abstract: A repeatable five-question drill that catches most design problems before the code review. We run it live on three real endpoints submitted by attendees. Bring a candidate endpoint if you want it dissected in public.

talks.title: Versioning without breaking clients
talks.abstract: Version numbers are cheap, client migrations are not. We compare three versioning strategies across a public API with ten thousand consumers and the deprecation policy each required. Practical guidance on additive change, sunset dates and the conversation with whoever owns the oldest integration.

talks.title: NFRs as a negotiation, not a checklist
talks.abstract: Non-functional requirements fail when they arrive as a list of numbers nobody owns. We reframe them as trade-offs with a named decider, a budget and a measurement method. Two case studies from a booking system show the difference in outcome.

talks.title: Latency budgets analysts can defend
talks.abstract: A p95 target is a promise about someone else's afternoon. We build a latency budget top-down from a user journey and defend it in a room full of engineers. Short, concrete and mostly arithmetic.

talks.title: Data modelling for messy reality
talks.abstract: Real source systems disagree with each other, and the canonical model usually loses. This talk covers slow-changing dimensions, late-arriving facts and the one table that saved a reporting project. Expect concrete DDL rather than theory.

talks.title: Where AI helps an analyst, and where it does not
talks.abstract: Six months of using language models inside a requirements practice, with the misses included. We separate drafting, summarising and clustering from the work that still needs a human in the room. A cost and quality comparison against the manual baseline.

talks.title: Stakeholder conflict: a facilitation script
talks.abstract: Two departments, one backlog and a standing disagreement about priority. We walk through a two-hour session designed to surface the real constraint and agree on a decision rule. The script is included and meant to be copied.

talks.title: Writing the one-page spec
talks.abstract: If it does not fit on one page, the reader will not read it. We take a bloated specification and cut it to a single page without losing the decisions. Template, exercises and the three sentences that most specs miss.
